reasons.reason: The Guarani is correct: oguata, akóinte (akói + -nte, accented because the stress is not on the last syllable), pe tape rupi. But «pe tape» means «ese camino». There is no diminutive for «caminito» and no word for «el mismo», so the gloss says more than the Guarani. The fix that carries the least risk is to make the gloss literal. In context (page 3 just said he goes to the arroyo), «ese camino» already means the same path. If the story should keep «mismo caminito», «Oguata akóinte upe tape'i rupi voi.» also follows the rules (tape + diminutive -'i, voi «mismo» after the phrase). The reviewers' «rupínte» changes the meaning to «only by».

reasons.best_es: Camina siempre por el mismo caminito.
reasons.reason: The spelling is correct (akóinte, rupi). In context, «akóinte pe tape rupi» («siempre por ese camino») means walking the same path every time, so «el mismo» is a fair idiomatic rendering, not a misleading one. The Spanish diminutive «caminito» is an affectionate tone for children, not a change of meaning. A teacher would not mark this. Both proposed fixes are worse. «upe tape'i rupi voi» puts voi awkwardly after the postpositional phrase, and it sounds unnatural. «akóinte ... rupínte» says «only/always» twice. Optional: if exact matching is wanted, the gloss could become «Camina siempre por ese camino.», but that is not needed.

why: This is a descriptive phrase inside a Spanish sentence, not a proper name, yet it uses title case: the capital on «Iñe'ẽporãhaipyre» after «ha» comes from the Spanish or English title habit. «Guarani Ñe'ẽ» can keep its capitals because it is the name of the MEC subject. «Mombe'u» is mainly the verb/root «contar, relatar». The usual school word for a story (cuento) is «mombe'urã» or «mombe'upy». Also, the gloss «Cuento del cielo» adds «del cielo», which is not in the Guarani.

«Mopu'ã» means to lift up, stand up or erect, as in mopu'ã óga «levantar una casa». Teachers do not usually say it for putting syllables together into a word. School materials say «embojoaju» (uní) or «ejapo» (hacé) for this.
The gloss says «Más guaraní», but the Guarani only says «Guarani». It does not show that this track is for children who hear more Guarani at home.
«Moõpa?» means only «¿Dónde?». The gloss adds «queda» and a subtitle, «Lugares y caminos», that the Guarani does not contain.
The title and gloss name only water and milk, but the lesson also teaches mbujape («pan»), so the title does not fully name what the lesson is.
Mombe'u is the verb or noun for «contar, relato». In school materials the literary genre «cuento» is usually mombe'urã, which is set against mombe'ugua'u «leyenda», the title of the next unit.

As a lesson title, «Che po» glossed «Mis manos» names only one of the four words taught (che juru, che nambi, che po, che py). The gloss is also plural, while the same phrase is glossed «Mi mano» inside the lesson and the word list.

Mba'éichapa? means «¿Cómo estás?» / «¿Qué tal?». The gloss adds «¡Hola!», which in this same unit is the meaning of Maitei (the unit title). A preschool child could take Mba'éichapa to be the word for «hola».
